text: Τὸ μὴ ἐξ ἀτελῶν. Variæ Græcis terminorum ac vocum acceptiones, quæ res in theologia difficultates parit, erroresque incautis innectit, uti quandoque ipse admonet Maximus. Exemplum istud quod adhibet τοῦ ἐνυποστάτου, paulo φυσικώτερον est. Ita sane in naturalibus, hypostasis ex imperfectis substantiis conflatur, ex quibus unum totum ac per se exsistens consurgit: in Christo autem utraque perfecta natura est; unde nec unum totum ut natura ex eis conflatur, sed unus perfectus Deus, perfectus homo in utraque exsistit; ipsasque non hypostases, sed ἐνυπόστατα alibi Maximus admittit. Hic vero quod ponit exemplum, de imperfecto quod perfecto utitur unione secundum confusionem, hoc forte velit. Partes, quæ sic accedunt perfecto, ex illa imperfecti cum eo mistione et confusione, ut sic ἐνυπόστατα esse, quæ vere in hypostasi cui adveniunt, exsistant, non ut accidentia, sed ut quid substantiale, nec extra hypostasim, etsi non sint ipsa hypostasis, quæ est totius ratio, ac per se seorsum a quocunque alio, exsistentis. Paulo post τὸ ἐνυπόστατον, ad ipsa trahit communia accidentia seu adventitia, quæ et ipsa in hypostasi exsistant: sed id remotius est, quod illa esse valde debile et secundum quid in ea habeant. Sequentia, excerpta potius sunt, ad sequentem usque epistolam ad Constantinum Sacellarium, quam justa aliqua lucubratio vel epistola; cumque ipsius Maximi nomine prænotati loci afferantur, conjectura sit ejus studiosum aliquem hæc potius quam ipsum Maximum digessisse; vel si primum Maximus digessit adversus Severianos et Monothelitas, sic illi digesta alius auxerit, uti fere aliqui exsistimant de quæst. ad Antiochum Athanasii nomine, deque Anastasii Sinaitæ in Scripturam, aliis Nicæni.
anchorLine: τουτέστι, τὸ μὴ ἐξ ἀτελῶν (h) μερῶν εἰς ἕν τι συνελ-
en: On 'not from imperfect [parts]': Greek terms and the senses of words vary, and this causes difficulty in theology and ensnares the unwary, as Maximus himself sometimes warns. The example he uses of 'enhypostaton' is rather natural. Thus in natural things a hypostasis is compounded from imperfect substances, out of which one whole, self-existing thing arises; but in Christ each nature is perfect, so that neither is one whole formed from them as a nature, but one perfect God, perfect man, exists in both; and Maximus elsewhere admits them to be 'enhypostata', not hypostases. Here, however, the example he sets down, of the imperfect that is used by the perfect by union according to confusion, he perhaps means this: parts that thus join the perfect, from the mixture and confusion of the imperfect with it, so as to be enhypostata, which exist truly in the hypostasis to which they come, not as accidents but as something substantial, and not outside the hypostasis, though they are not the hypostasis itself, which is that of the whole and exists separately by itself from anything else. A little later he draws 'enhypostaton' to the common accidents or adventitious things, which also exist in the hypostasis; but that is more remote, since they have it only very weakly and in a qualified way. What follows is rather excerpts, as far as the next letter to Constantine the Sacellarius, than a proper treatise or letter; and since the passages are cited under Maximus's name, the conjecture is that some student composed these rather than Maximus himself, or, if Maximus first composed them against the Severians and Monothelites, that another enlarged his compilations, as some commonly suppose of the question to Antiochus under Athanasius's name, and of Anastasius of Sinai on Scripture, and others of the Nicene.

text: Εἰ διὰ τὸ ἓν θέλημα. Non b[…]e Turr., inter cujus Maximi opuscula istud undecimum est, istam sententiam superiori jungit; quo cogitur decimam numerare, quod epilogi rationem habet. Habuerit ejus cod. εἶτα, εἰ, quod ille reddit, Deinde, si: nihil tamen id favet, ut non sit nova sententia seu argumentum, quæ alia aliis subnectere solent Græci ejusmodi particulis, uti fere etiam Latini. Titulus in Turr. cod. et Romano paulo diversus: illius est, Γνῶμαι ἀποδεικτικαὶ περὶ τῶν δύο τοῦ Χριστοῦ θελημάτων, Romani, qualem repræsentavi.
anchorLine: ς΄. Εἰ διὰ τὸ ἓν θέλημα (i) Πατρὸς καὶ Υἱοῦ καὶ
en: On "Εἰ διὰ τὸ ἓν θέλημα": [one or two letters of the third word lost] in the Turin codex, in which this opusculum of Maximus is the eleventh, it joins this sentence to the one above; hence it is forced to count a tenth, which has the force of an epilogue. His codex may have had εἶτα (then) for εἰ (if), which he rendered "Then, if": yet that does not prevent this from being a new sentence or argument, such as Greeks, and Latins too, commonly append with such particles. The title in the Turin codex and in the Roman differs a little: that of the former is "Γνῶμαι ἀποδεικτικαὶ περὶ τῶν δύο τοῦ Χριστοῦ θελημάτων" (demonstrative sentences on the two wills of Christ), that of the Roman is the one I have given.

text: desiderant Turr. codex, ipsæ videntur, quæ hic subjectæ sunt, post breve illud excerptum Responsionum ad Theodorum presbyterum; uti etiam censuit vir cl. Lucas Holstenius, ac Roma scripsit: Imo ipsæ sunt quibus Maximus abunde fidem liberat, Patrumque doctrinam ac traditionem de naturali voluntate et operatione sic enucleate, tanta vi ac copia promit, ut ad ejus operam nihil desiderari videatur; plenissimeque ea retundantur impudentissima Sergii, Pauli, aliorumque Monothelitarum hæresis antistitum ora, qui vel Patres illius non meminisse jactabant, vel ἀδιάφορον habendum volebant, sive una, sive duplex operatio atque voluntas dicetur, quasi neutrum ad fidem spectaret, satisque ei consultum esset, dissidentium parti[…] silentio; quod et Honorio primum sancitum, tum[…] circumscribente Sergio, ut loquitur Christianu[…] Lupus, tum quod ea indulgentia Theodosiano[…] aliosque Severianos adducendos speraret. Eju[…] tamen decretum nemini successorum probatum[…] excusatus animos, ne pari cum Ecthesi ac Typo[…] synodo Lateranensi calculo notaretur. Longa seri[…] refert laudatus Lupus c. 5 Notarum ad vi synodum, eos qui eadem locuti cum hæreticis, ipsaque[…] in illis proscripta, ipsi tamen hæreticis minime adscripti sunt, ac quæ sic locuti sunt, benignius habita.
en: [Continuing the note on "Διαβεβαιοῦνται" from the previous page:] ...and which the Turin codex lacks, seem to be those which are subjoined here, after the short excerpt of the Replies to Theodore the presbyter, as the distinguished Lucas Holstenius judged, and wrote from Rome. Nay, rather they are the very ones by which Maximus abundantly frees his credit, setting out the doctrine and tradition of the Fathers on natural will and operation with such force and richness that nothing seems wanting to his work; and by them the most shameless mouths of Sergius, Paul and the other leaders of the Monothelite heresy are most fully refuted, who either boasted that the Fathers made no mention of it, or wished it held a matter of indifference whether one or two operations and wills be spoken of, as though neither bore on the faith, and enough had been provided for him by silence of the dissenting parties[…]; which was first decreed by Honorius, and then, as Christian Lupus says, by Sergius's circumvention, and because by that indulgence he hoped the Theodosians and other Severians could be brought over. Yet his decree was approved by none of his successors; [and he is] excused in intention, lest he be marked by the judgment of the Lateran synod as equal with the Ecthesis and Typus. The cited Lupus, ch. 5 of his Notes, relates at length, on the sixth synod, that those who said the same things as the heretics, and whose [words] were proscribed among them, were nevertheless by no means counted among the heretics, and that what they thus said was taken more kindly.
